name: Event Sourcing
intent: Store every change as an immutable event and derive the current state by replaying them, instead of storing only the latest state.
scenario: A bank account normally stores just a balance. Auditors ask how it reached that number, and a bug has produced a wrong one that nobody can explain.
problem: When you overwrite the current state, the history is gone. You cannot answer 'how did we get here?', cannot reproduce a past bug, and cannot rebuild a corrupted or differently shaped view of the data. Updates in place also make it hard to attach other systems that need to react to every change.

howItWorks.title: Record facts, not state
howItWorks.text: A command such as 'withdraw 30' is first validated against the current state. If it is allowed, the system appends an event (Withdrawn 30) to an append-only log. Events are named in the past tense and are never edited or deleted.

howItWorks.title: Current state is a fold of the events
howItWorks.text: To know the balance, start from zero and apply every event in order. Rebuilding state from the log always gives the same answer, because each event simply says what happened.

howItWorks.title: Snapshots keep replay short
howItWorks.text: Replaying millions of events for every request is slow. Periodically the system stores a snapshot (the state at event N). To load, take the latest snapshot and replay only the events after it.

howItWorks.title: The log is a source for many views
howItWorks.text: Other components (projections) read the events and build whatever shape they need: a balance table, a search index, a report. A new view can be created later by replaying history from the start. This pairs naturally with CQRS and pub/sub.

howItWorks.title: Mistakes are corrected with new events
howItWorks.text: Because history is immutable you fix a wrong entry by appending a compensating event (a reversal), not by editing the past. That keeps a complete, trustworthy audit trail, and lets you ask 'what was the state at time T?'.

pros: Can rebuild state, or reproduce a bug, at any point in the past
New read models and reports can be derived later from old events
cons: A different way of thinking, with a real learning curve
Queries on current state need projections, which are eventually consistent
Event schemas must be versioned for years, since old events live forever
Replay, snapshots and storage growth need engineering
whenToUse: Domains where history matters: finance, orders, bookings, compliance
You need audit, debugging by replay, or temporal queries
Several different views of the same data are needed
Business events are already the natural language of the domain
whenNotToUse: Simple CRUD where only the latest value matters
Data you must erase for privacy reasons, because an immutable log fights deletion (design for this explicitly)
Small teams without the appetite for the extra moving parts
pitfalls: Putting derived or unstable data in events, which makes replay fragile
Changing the meaning of an old event type instead of versioning it
Replaying side effects (sending emails again) while rebuilding state
Using event sourcing for the whole system when only a few parts need it
